full_judgment:
Md A Wahhab Miah J: In this petition, the petitioner who is the heir of the deceased defendant, Md. Yousuf Chowdhury has called in question the judgment and decree dated the 20th day of May, 2010 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 199 of 1992 dismissing the same. 

 5. The trial Court by judgment and decree dated 16-3-1992 decreed the suit. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the trial Court, the defendant filed the above mentioned first appeal before the High Court Division. A Division Bench of the High Court Division on hearing the appeal by the impugned judgment and decree dismissed the same concurring with the finding of the trial Court; hence this petition for leave to appeal. 

 7. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Advocate, entering caveat on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent, on the other hand, supported the impugned judgment and decree on the submission that the High Court Division being the last Court of fact concurred with the findings of the trial Court as to the execution of the agreement by the defendant for selling the suit property and passing of consideration to the defendant and the readiness of the plaintiff to get the kabala executed and registered by paying the balance money of Taka 11,000, there is no scope of interference by this Division with the impugned judgment and decree and the leave petition be dismissed. 

 8. We have gone through the judgment and decree of the trial Court and that of the High Court Division. Admittedly, the defendant executed the agreement and the same is a registered one. As per own admission of the defendant, he took Taka 1,25,000 from the plaintiff on the date of execution of the agreement. The case of the defendant is that he took the said money as a loan for his business purpose for 1(one) year with the condition to pay interest of Taka 15,000 and executed the agreement as a security of the said loan and that he returned back most of the money to the plaintiff on different dates which were duly noted in his diary, so onus was heavily upon him to prove the said case in view of the fact that the agreement was a registered one. From the judgment and decree of the trial Court, it appears that it considered every bit of evidence, both oral and documentary, and came to the specific finding that the defendant entered into an agreement with the plaintiff for selling the suit property at the highest market price of Taka 2,00,000 (two lac) at the relevant time and on receipt of Taka 1,50,000 as advance executed and registered the agreement. The trial Court further held that the case of the defendant that he returned back most of the money to the plaintiff which he took from him as loan which had been shown in the alleged agreement as advance for selling the suit property was not correct. The trial Court further held that no hardship would be caused to the defendant if the suit was decreed. The High Court Division as the last Court of fact concurred with those findings of the trial Court with the observation that since the agreement was a registered one, it had a presumptive value and the onus was heavily upon the defendant to prove his case that, in fact, it was not an agreement for sale of the suit property, but was executed as a security for the loan taken by him from the plaintiff and that he paid most of the money to the plaintiff.
